column2: Having known the place, time and enjoyment, and the strength and weakness in a loss, those skilled in goods should state what is to be paid, without doubt.
One forced into slavery by thieves and also sold is freed; one who saves his master's life, from abandoning the devotion, also by ransom;
one who has fallen from renunciation is the king's slave till death; slavery is in the order of castes, not against the order.
Even one who has completed his craft should stay for the stipulated time in the teacher's house; the resident pupil, with food from the teacher, gives the fruit of that.
The king, having made a place in the city and settled Brahmins there, should say to the one with livelihood in the three Vedas: "Let your own dharma be maintained."
One who is bound by contract without conflict with his own dharma, he too is to be protected with effort, and the dharma made by the king.
One who takes a guild's property and who breaks an agreement, having confiscated all his property, one should banish him from the kingdom.
The word of those speaking for the benefit of the group should be done by all; whoever is contrary there should first be made to pay a fine.
One sent on the group's business should hand over whatever he gets; if he does not hand it over himself, he is to pay eleven-fold.
They should be Veda-knowers, pure, free of greed, thinkers of the business; the word of those speaking for the group's good is to be followed.
This rule applies also to guilds, merchant bodies, sects and groups. The king should protect their division and maintain their former conduct.
One who has taken wages and abandons the work should pay double; if not taken, equal; the servants should protect the equipment.
A tenth part should be paid from trade, cattle and crops. One who has work done without fixing the wage,
who exceeds the place and time, or does the work otherwise, there the master's wish — more should be given for more work done.
As much work as one does, so much is his wage. If both cannot settle it, he should do the possible as agreed.
A carrier should pay for goods lost without king's or fate's cause; one who obstructs departure should pay double wage.
When he has begun, a seventh part; abandoning on the road, a fourth; abandoning at half the road, the whole wage should be paid.
In a wager, a hundred with interest: the gambling-house keeper takes five; from rogue gamblers ten per hundred;
he, well protected, should give the king a share as arranged. He should make the winnings collected and give them to the winner, being forgiving and truthful.
When the king's share is obtained among a known gang of rogues, he should have the winnings paid in the gaming-hall place, not otherwise.
The overseers of the dealings and the witnesses are those same; false dice-players and cheaters should be banished by the king, marked.
Gambling should be made single-faced for the purpose of knowing thieves. The same rule is to be known in betting on living beings and challenges.
On cutting all of the branches and trunks of growing trees; of useful trees, twenty, double the fines.
One who has violence done should pay double the fine; one who says "I am the giver" and has it done, fourfold.
One who transgresses against a noble lady, one who strikes a brother's wife, one who does not give what was directed, one who breaks sea-houses,
one who does harm to neighbors, family members and the like: a fifty-pana fine is decided for these.
One who goes to a self-willed widow; one who does not run when cried to; one who cries without cause; a Chandala touching the high;
a Shudra feeding renunciants at divine and ancestral rites; one who swears an improper oath; the unfit doing fit work;
one who harms the manhood of bulls and small animals; one who cheats a common property; one who destroys the pregnancy of a slave-woman;
father and son, sisters and brother, married pair, teacher and pupil — one who abandons another of these when not fallen is liable to a hundred fine.
A washerman wearing another's cloth: three panas; for sale, barter, deposit and loan: ten panas.
A forger of balances, edicts, measures and coin, and one who deals with these should be made to pay the highest fine.
One who calls the genuine false and the false genuine: the coin-tester should be made to pay the first-degree fine.
A physician acting wrongly should pay the first fine for animals; the middle for humans; the highest for the king's men.
One who binds the unbindable, releases the bindable, and one with improper legal action, should pay the highest fine.
One who takes an eighth part by measure or balance should pay twenty-two panas; the loss and gain are as reckoned.
One who adds inferior stuff to goods such as medicine, oil, salt, scents, grain and jaggery should pay sixteen panas.
Craftsmen who combine and obstruct to raise or lower the price of goods, a thousand fine is said.
What is set by the king, by that selling is daily; purchase or outflow therefrom is remembered as making merchants' profit.
A merchant should take a hundred, five on local goods, ten on foreign, who buys and sells at once;
having set the expense arising from goods on the goods, a benefit should be made for both buyer and seller.
One who does not give the buyer the goods whose price he has taken should pay with interest, or, if he came from abroad, the profit.
Even sold goods may be resold if the earlier buyer does not take them; if loss occurs by the buyer's fault, it is the buyer's own.
If fault arises in goods by calamity from king or fate, the loss is the seller's, if he refuses when requested.
If sold into another's hand, or bad as if bad — if he sells, the fine there shall be double its price.
A merchant not knowing the loss and gain of goods should not regret after buying; doing so he is liable to a sixth-part fine.
For merchants who act jointly for profit, profit and loss are as in the property or as made by agreement.
What is forbidden, not ordered, or destroyed through negligence, he should pay that; and from the protected, a tenth share.
The king should take a twentieth part as toll on goods for sale; what is smuggled and fit for the king, if sold, goes to the king.
One who speaks falsely of the measure, who slips away from the toll-post, and in fraudulent purchase and sale should pay eightfold.
When one has died gone to another country, his heirs, relatives or kinsmen should take the goods; those who come, or the king without them.
They should abandon crookedness; the unable should have it done by another without greed. By this the rule is stated for priests, farmers and workmen.
A thief is seized by seekers with the stolen goods or the footprint; or one guilty of former crime, or likewise an impure resident;
others too are to be seized on suspicion by denial of caste, name and the like; the addicted to dice, women and drink, with dry and broken voice and mouth,
inquirers about others' property and houses, secret wanderers, without income and with expense, and sellers of ruined goods.
One seized on suspicion of theft, if he clears himself, having made him pay the stolen goods, one should punish with a thief's fine.
Having made a thief pay what was taken, the wise should have him killed by various means; a Brahmin one should mark and banish from his kingdom.
In killing and robbery, the fault of the village lord who did not go out: the village should pay within its boundary, or where the track goes;
of five villages beyond a krosha, or of ten villages — for prisoner-takers, and thieves of horses and elephants,
and violent killers, one should impale such men. The pickpocket and knot-cutter, without hand and thumb,
should be made so; on the second offence missing a hand and foot. Having given the meal, shelter, fire, water, mantra and equipment expenses,
to a thief, or a knowing killer, the highest fine. For dropping a weapon or causing miscarriage, the highest fine;
for killing a man or a woman, whether highest or lowest: binding a stone, one should throw into water a woman who killed a man or gave poison;
a woman who gave poison or fire, killed her own teacher or own child, having cut ears, hands, nose and lips, one should have her killed with cows.
Those who burn fields, houses, forests, villages, pastures and threshing floors, and one who goes to the king's wife, should be burned in a straw fire.
A man who embraces another's wife (hair to hair) is to be seized; in one's own caste the highest fine; in the natural order the middle;
in the reverse order death for men; for women the cutting of the ears; pulling at the waistband, breast, covering, navel or hair —
speaking at a wrong place and time, and staying together: if a woman refuses, a hundred she should give; a man, a two-hundred fine;
the penalty on both for refusal is as for embracing. One who goes to animals should pay a hundred; to a low woman or cows, the middle;
among enclosed slave women and likewise among kept women — even in those fit to be gone to the man should pay a fifty-pana fine.
In going to a slave woman by force the fine is remembered as ten panas; one who goes to a low-caste or renunciant woman should be branded with a bad brand and sent away.
One who writes a royal order with less or more, or who releases an adulterer or a thief, gets the highest fine.
One polluting a Brahmin with forbidden food: the highest fine of violence; a dealer in false gold and a seller of bad flesh
should be made limbless and made to pay the highest fine. An owner who is able and does not restrain fanged and horned animals
should pay the first fine, and double if it was cried out; one who accuses a non-thief as a thief should be made to pay a five-hundred fine.
